title: Lower Leg Anatomy and Clinical Relevance
subject: Anatomy
summary: The lower leg contains the tibia, fibula, and a complex network of muscles, nerves and vessels. Clinically, its anatomy guides the diagnosis of fractures, vascular disease, infections and pressure ulcers common in low‑resource settings.

sections.p: The lower leg is the segment between the knee and the ankle, comprising bone, muscle, nerve and vascular structures that support ambulation and maintain venous return.
b: Tibia and fibula form the skeleton
Muscle compartments: anterior, lateral, deep posterior, superficial posterior
Saphenous nerve supplies sensation to medial leg

sections.p: The tibia is the weight‑bearing bone; the fibula is thinner and provides attachment for muscles and ligaments.
The lower leg lies posterior to the thigh and anterior to the foot. Key relations include the popliteal fossa behind, the tibial nerve and artery medially, and the peroneal nerve laterally.
b: Saphenous vein runs with saphenous nerve
Peroneal nerve wraps around fibular head

sections.p: The popliteal artery bifurcates into the anterior tibial, posterior tibial and peroneal arteries, supplying the compartments.

t.b: Assesses anterior tibial artery patency; loss of dorsiflexion suggests arterial insufficiency.

sections.p: Sensory: saphenous nerve (medial leg), superficial peroneal nerve (lateral leg). Motor: deep peroneal (extensors), tibial nerve (flexors).
b: Loss of sensation over medial malleolus = saphenous neuropathy
Foot drop = deep peroneal nerve injury

sections.p: Supports weight, facilitates gait, and protects the ankle joint. Muscle compartments allow flexion, extension, inversion and eversion.
Fractures, compartment syndrome, venous stasis, infections (tetanus, cellulitis), pressure ulcers and peripheral arterial disease are common.
b: Low‑resource settings see malaria‑related anemia leading to leg swelling

t.b: Detects peripheral arterial disease; absent pulse indicates severe occlusion.
Screen for chronic venous insufficiency; >34 cm suggests significant edema.
Elevated in cellulitis; normal in early venous stasis.

sections.p: Use a systematic approach: history of trauma, vascular risk factors, infection signs, and ulcer characteristics. Check pulses, capillary refill, skin temperature and color.
b: Ask about recent falls or infections
Palpate for tenderness and compartment pressure if suspected

sections.p: Differential includes deep vein thrombosis, cellulitis, venous stasis, and pressure ulcer.
b: DVT: pain, swelling, calf tenderness, positive Homan sign

sections.p: In malaria endemic areas, anemia can mask hypovolemia; low-grade fever may be missed in chronic infections.
b: Normal WCC can occur in early cellulitis

sections.p: Treat underlying cause: antibiotics for infection, anticoagulation for DVT, surgical decompression for compartment syndrome. Supportive care includes elevation, compression stockings and wound care.
Urgent referral if sudden severe pain, swelling, loss of pulses, or signs of systemic infection.
b: Pain out of proportion to injury

faq.a: Increased pressure within a muscle compartment that compromises circulation and nerve function.

faq.q: How do you differentiate venous stasis from cellulitis?
faq.a: Venous stasis: chronic, painless swelling, skin changes; cellulitis: acute pain, warmth, erythema, fever.

faq.q: Why is the saphenous nerve important?
faq.a: It provides sensation to the medial leg; injury can cause numbness and affect wound care.

exam: A 35‑year‑old man presents with a swollen, painful left calf after a fall. What is the next best step? — Check pulses, perform a Doppler, and if pulses are absent, arrange urgent vascular imaging.
A 50‑year‑old diabetic woman has a non‑healing ulcer above the medial malleolus. What is the first investigation? — X‑ray to rule out osteomyelitis; if negative, start wound care and compression.

A 28‑year‑old woman with sudden calf pain and swelling after a long flight. What is the most likely diagnosis and immediate management? — Deep vein thrombosis; give low‑molecular‑weight heparin and refer for ultrasound.
A 60‑year‑old man with chronic leg swelling and shiny skin. What is the most likely cause? — Chronic venous insufficiency; assess ankle‑brachial index and start compression therapy.
A 45‑year‑old man with a tibial fracture and increasing pain out of proportion to injury. What is the emergency treatment? — Suspect compartment syndrome; perform immediate fasciotomy.
A 70‑year‑old woman with a painless ulcer on the foot. What is the differential? — Peripheral arterial disease, neuropathy, and pressure ulcer; assess pulses and sensory testing.
